title: Physiological Indicators of Trail Running Performance: A Systematic Review
authors: de Waal SJ, Gomez-Ezeiza J, Venter RE, Lamberts RP
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
findings: Trail performance most often correlated with maximal aerobic capacity (71% of studies; r = -.50), lactate threshold (57%; r = -.48), velocity at maximal aerobic capacity (43%; r = -.68), running economy (43%; r = -.31), body fat (43%; r = .55) and age (43%; r = .52).
Regression models explained 48-60% (single variable) and 48-99% (multiple variable) of performance variation.
The classic endurance model is a weaker predictor in trail than in road running.
Testing procedures, race profiles and participants differ so much that comparisons are hindered.
limitations: Only 7 studies; the abstract states that testing procedures, race profiles and participants differ so much that comparisons are hindered. No meta-analysis is reported. The abstract does not state the sign convention of the correlations, which are presumably against finishing time (negative r = faster).
implications: Do not predict trail finishing times from a road-based VO2max or flat-pace model alone; the classic endurance model was a weaker predictor in trail than in road running, so widen the prediction interval for trail goals.
Where the runner has trail-specific data (graded running economy, actual race splits on known gradients), prefer it over road-derived values and label trail predictions as lower confidence.

verification.notes: Crossref: Int J Sports Physiol Perform 16(3):325-332, 2021, four authors match. PubMed PMID 33508776 abstract supports all numbers (percentages read as share of the 7 studies: 5/7=71%, 4/7=57%, 3/7=43%). A systematic review by design (A), but of 7 heterogeneous studies; strength limited.
